Let’s dive into Chapter 4: Challenging the Food Police and Embracing Body Respect.
As your relationship with food gets a little more peaceful, there’s often a new challenge that pops up—the internal “food police.” You know, that critical voice in your head that comments on every bite and seems to measure your worthiness by what you eat?
The food police aren’t just something you’re born with—they’re shaped by years of diet culture, family messages, and all those expectations society throws at us. Maybe you’ve heard that voice whisper, “You shouldn’t eat that,” or, “Well, you’ve already ruined your day.” It keeps score, counting up calories or “sins,” and treats food choices like a test of self-control. Everything becomes black or white—foods are “good” or “bad,” and, somehow, you’re supposed to be perfect all the time.
Here’s something to really pay attention to: challenging the food police means recognizing those thoughts for what they are—learned habits, not your body’s real needs. They’re just echoes of rules you’ve picked up along the way, not the truth about what you actually need or want.
So, how do you quiet that relentless critic? It starts with a few gentle strategies:
First, try naming the critical voice. When you can call it the “food police,” it’s a little easier to separate yourself from all that judgment.
Next, swap criticism for curiosity. Instead of thinking, “I shouldn’t have eaten that,” you might ask yourself, “What was I feeling, or needing, in that moment?” It’s not about blame—it’s about understanding.
Remember, all foods are allowed. Eating isn’t a moral issue. Giving yourself permission to eat can be so freeing.
And most of all, practice self-talk that’s kind and supportive—especially after you eat something you used to label as “bad.” Imagine speaking to yourself the way you’d comfort a friend.
Right alongside challenging the food police comes the idea of body respect. This doesn’t mean you have to love your body every second, or be endlessly positive. Instead, it’s about caring for your body as it is, right now—not waiting for it to change first.
Body respect can show up in so many ways. Maybe it’s choosing clothes that actually fit comfortably, instead of squeezing into old jeans as some kind of punishment. Or it’s making sure you’re nourishing yourself with regular meals and snacks, instead of skipping food to stay in control. It could even mean moving your body in ways that feel good, instead of turning exercise into a form of payback.
And most importantly—talk to yourself with the same respect and care you’d offer someone you love.
Here’s a powerful truth: bodies come in all shapes and sizes, and health isn’t defined by weight alone. In fact, research shows that constantly losing and regaining weight—what’s called weight cycling—can be more harmful than simply maintaining a stable weight, even if it’s higher than what culture considers “ideal.”
Let’s put this into real life. Imagine someone who used to skip out on social events, terrified of being surrounded by “bad” foods. Over time, they start showing up, feeling more at ease, and just enjoying the moment. Or maybe it’s the person who finally lets go of those too-tight jeans, donates them, and buys clothes that truly fit—discovering a new sense of comfort and confidence.
Challenging the food police and practicing body respect aren’t quick fixes—they’re ongoing, and sometimes tough. But with patience, persistence, and a willingness to question those old beliefs, that critical voice gets quieter. In its place, you’ll start to find a sense of peace and real self-acceptance.
